newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten says will work till the very end of HK rule.
newsitem.headline: Patten says will work till the very end of HK rule.

text.p: Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten, long blasted by Beijing as a "political prostitute", vowed on Thursday to keep his meet-the-people tours going until the final hours of colonial rule on June 30.

Patten broke a long tradition when he arrived in Hong Kong in 1992 after losing his parliamentary seat in a British general election. He refused to wear a governor's uniform with its cockaded pith helmet.
After generations of aloof rulers from London, the territory of 6.4 million people welcomed his gesture as demonstrating a common touch and got used to an easygoing leader in a business suit.

His popularity, boosted by democratic reform, rose here as it sank in the Chinese capital where news media said he would be condemned for "10,000 generations" for changing the political structure without China's blessing.
Following his initial coup, the well-nourished Patten became known familiarly as "Fatty" in Cantonese. But he slimmed down after a 1993 heart operation.
The first career-politician to govern Hong Kong, Patten is used to glad-handing and baby-kissing when he meets the people.
And he says he will keep going right to the end of the road.
He constantly makes unannounced visits to public housing estates where he chats with ordinary people, on a scale seldom seen in the 156-year history of the colony.

His informality contrasts with his post-colonial successor, Tung Chee-hwa, a former shipping tycoon chosen by a China-assembled committee to run Hong Kong after the British withdraw. Tung appears uptight in the public spotlight.

"I will continue to make community visits until the mid-morning of June 30," Patten told reporters after visiting a hostel for the mentally handicapped and a public housing estate in southern Hong Kong island.
He said such visits gave Hong Kong people a chance to meet him and made him more aware of the everyday problems in Hong Kong.
During Thursday's walkabout, he turned his hand to cuisine, an old favourite, and joined residents in making Chinese dumplings for a Dragon Boat Festival on Monday.
Experts say the dumpling wrapped by the 28th and last governor wasn't as good as those made by the hostel residents but they saluted his effort with a thumbs-up signal.
He was also asked by a reporter to autograph a copy of "Hong Kong 1997", the last yearbook put out by the colonial administration, with a foreword written by the governor himself.
He did so. "It might be worth a lot of money," fellow reporters said enviously.
